newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU REJECTS CLABECQ RESCUE PLAN.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU REJECTS CLABECQ RESCUE PLAN.

text.p: The European Commission on Wednesday rejected a rescue plan by Belgium's Walloon region for loss-making steel firm Forges de Clabecq but said it would help the industrially depressed area attract new investment.
"The Commission has declared that the measures taken by the Walloon region in favour of Forges de Clabecq...are incompatible with the common market," a Commission statement said.

The measures refered to Wallonia's offer of 1.5 billion ($46.9 million) Belgian francs of capital, 700 million francs of credit already granted, the writing off of debts worth more than 800 million francs and the rescheduling of other borrowings.

The Commission said the subsidies went against EU rules which only allowed steel aid for environmental reasons, for research and development or for company closure. The money already received by Clabecq must be paid back within two months.
Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told a news conference, however, the Commission "will use the means available to it to help the Walloon region do the necessary reconversion."

"Although the decision might be called a negative one, there is a positive signal going out that the maximum will be done to help the region to attract other investment which is more likely to bear fruit."

Reacting to the decision Minister-President of the Walloon regional government Robert Collignon said in a statement he "vigorously reaffirmed his willingness to look at all solutions aimed at keeping significant steel activity going at Clabecq."
He deeply regretted the Commission's ruling, and noted the rescue plan had involved capacity cuts.

Despite the prospect of help for the region, analysts said the deathknell had been sounded for loss-making Clabecq which has struggled in a volatile market marked by overcapacity and failed to find a partner to improve its position.

"This is the end for Clabecq. It seems neither of the other two steel companies (Dutch Hoogovens and Belgian Usines Gustave Boel) are interested in taking over any part of Clabecq," said steel analyst Patrik Geldermans at Kredietbank.

Hoogovens is planning a 50-50 joint venture with UGB whose activities, it says, complement its own business. Belgium's largest steelmaker Cockerill Sambre has already ruled out partnerships with UGB and Clabecq.

Van Miert noted that when the Clabecq rescue plan was launched the company was near to bankruptcy, and a report commissioned by the Walloon region, the majority shareholder in Clabecq and Cockerill, said Clabecq was unlikely to survive.
The report showed Clabecq's costs were 20 to 30 percent above the average of its competitors.
Analysts said that the company had also been saddled with poor operational margins and low-quality products.

In slimmed-down form, with debts restructured, Clabecq might make a new start but not without a severe impact on 1,700 people directly employed and the 3,500 whose jobs are linked to the steel firm, they added.
Clabecq closed at 91 francs on the Brussels bourse on Tuesday, but the indicative price plunged on Wednesday to 20 francs.
The share price has been falling steadily since June when it was at 380 francs and the bourse has imposed a 10 percent maximum markdown a day due to the excess of sellers.
Indicating the firms's problems, its book value per share stands at a negative 850 francs. By contrast, healthy Cockerill Sambre has a book value per share of 980 francs.
